    (function () {
      function playerFor(h, v) {
        return document.getElementById('audioplayer-' + h + '.' + v);

      function prime(a) {
        if (!a) return;
        if (a.readyState === 0) { try { a.load(); } catch (e) {} }

        return playerFor(i.h, i.v || 0);

      }

        if (window.Reveal && Reveal.on) {
          Reveal.on('slidechanged', function () { prime(currentPlayer()); });

        if (document.getElementById('audio-start')) return;

          'background:rgba(255,255,255,.92);text-align:center';
        d.addEventListener('click', function () { start(); d.remove(); });
        document.body.appendChild(d);
      }
      if (document.readyState === 'loading') {
        document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', arm);
      } else { arm(); }
    })();
    </script>

## This talk, in three pictures

::: figgrid
<figure>
<img src="images/sec-full.jpg">
<figcaption><b>1.</b> The covariance step now covers every parameter</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure>
<img src="images/sec-any.jpg">
<figcaption><b>2.</b> sa and imp break free of one estimation method</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure>
<img src="images/sec-analytic.jpg">
<figcaption><b>3.</b> The analytic covariance: an exact standard error</figcaption>
</figure>
:::

::: {.notes}
Three things changed in the covariance step for this release:

1. The default covariance step now covers every parameter.

2. Two new covariance methods, SA and IMP that can be used almost anywhere.

3. A genuine new covariance method Hidde create -- an exact analytic covariance
:::

## 1. A full covariance step {.sectionbreak}

![](images/sec-full.jpg){.nostretch}

::: {.notes}
Let's start with the covariance step now full covariances are created
:::

::: {.notes}

Now the additive residual error standard deviation is calculated on
all methods -- before 7.0 the standard error was missing.
:::

## That was a deliberate choice, not an oversight

- We, as a nlmixr2 team, think that when you simulate *with* uncertainty,
  the `omega` and `sigma` terms should be simulated from the inverse
  Wishart distribution, not from standard errors
- Getting real `omega` and residual standard errors also required
  meaningfully more implementation effort than the approach we
  originally took

::: rule
:::

7.0 adds the full covariance step *on top of* that -- it is not a reversal
of how we think about simulating uncertainty.

::: {.notes}
We've always leaned toward the inverse Wishart distribution for
simulating uncertainty in omega and sigma; we hoped not having these
standard errors this would lead others to do that as well.

Additionally, getting real standard errors for those terms took real
additional work.

This new work really doesn't change how we think simulating with
uncertainty.

However, these values inform how well these parameters are estimated
and are frequently requested (and useful in other methods).
:::

## Fit the model, and `add.sd` comes back with a real number

```r
fit <- nlmixr2(pheno, pheno_sd, est="focei")
print(fit)
```

::: {.smaller}
`add.sd` -- SE about `0.008`, roughly 0.9% RSE -- a number that, before
this release, simply was not there.
:::

::: rule
:::

```r
fit$cov
```

::: {.smaller}
The full covariance (`$cov`) also carries the `Omega` block, named by
random effect -- `om.eta.cl`, `cov.eta.cl.eta.v` -- so you can find what
you're looking for without guessing at row order.
:::

::: {.notes}
A tight standard error is produced for this method. If you look at the
full covariance matrix, you'll also see the omega block, and every row
is named by the random effect it belongs to, so you're never guessing
at row order.
:::

## Only three things still don't get a standard error

::: {.checks}
- Everything else -- structural, covariate, and residual-error thetas
:::

- `fix()`ed parameters -- there is nothing to estimate a standard error for
- inter-occasion variability (IOV) parameters -- those are individual-level,
  not population-level
- mixture-probability parameters on the mlogit scale -- yes, we have
  mixtures now too, more on that another day

::: {.notes}
So what's still skipped. Fixed parameters, Inter occasion variability
parameters and mixture probability Everything else is in.
:::

## 2. `sa` and `imp` break free of one estimation method {.sectionbreak}

![](images/sec-any.jpg){.nostretch}

::: {.notes}
The second change is bigger than it sounds: two covariance methods
stopped being tied to one specific estimation method.
:::

::: {.notes}

The new SA and IMP covariance methods can be requested for practically
any fit and also be computed post fit, at the converged estimates of
any mixed effects fit.
:::

## `setCov()` switches a finished fit without refitting anything

```r
fit <- nlmixr2(pheno, pheno_sd, est="focei")

# the SAEM Louis stochastic-approximation FIM, on a focei fit,
# without refitting anything
setCov(fit, "sa")

# the importance-sampling Monte Carlo observed information, same fit
setCov(fit, "imp")
```

::: {.smaller}
`setCov()` calculates the covariance and installs it on the fit. Once
calculated, it is saved, so switching back and forth costs nothing extra.
:::

::: {.notes}
setCov calculates the new covariance and folds it right into the fit.
Once it's calculated, it's cached, so you can flip between covariance
methods on the same fit without paying the calculation cost twice.
:::

## `covMethod` is now a shared vocabulary of nine tokens

::: {.bigtable}

| token | what it is |
|---|---|
| `"r,s"` | sandwich, `solve(R) %*% S %*% solve(R)` -- the `focei`-family default |
| `"r"` / `"s"` | just the Hessian half or the cross-product half of the sandwich |
| `"analytic"` | exact observed-information covariance, matches NONMEM's `$COV MATRIX=R` |
| `"sa"` | SAEM Louis stochastic-approximation FIM (Kuhn & Lavielle 2005) |
| `"imp"` | importance-sampling Monte Carlo observed information |
| `"vi"` | variational covariance -- `emvi`/`fbvi` only |
| `"nlme"` | `nlme`'s own standard errors -- `nlme` only |
| `"linFim"` / `"fim"` | SAEM's linearized / accumulated Fisher information -- `saem` only |
| `""` | skip the covariance step |

:::

::: {.notes}
Here's the full vocabulary. R comma S is the sandwich estimator, and it's
the default for the focei family. Analytic is the exact observed
information, matching NONMEM's COV MATRIX equals R. SAEM's Louis
stochastic approximation Fisher information and the importance sampling
Monte Carlo observed information are the two that travel across methods.
The rest stay tied to their own method -- the variational covariance,
nlme's own standard errors, and SAEM's linearized and accumulated Fisher
information, all listed on the slide. And an empty string just skips the
covariance step.
:::

## Most families' defaults now reflect what they're actually best at

::: {.bigtable}

| family | default `covMethod` | note |
|---|---|---|
| `focei` / `foce` / `laplace` / `agq` | `"r,s"` | unchanged |
| `saem` | `"sa"` | falls back `"analytic"` then `"linFim"` when out of scope |
| `imp` / `impmap` / `qrpem` | `"imp"` | `impCov=TRUE` argument is gone -- this is just the default now |
| `nlme` | `"nlme"` | unchanged, but `"analytic"` is now selectable too |
| `npag` / `npb` | `"imp"` | currently does not have its own method  |
| `emvi` / `fbvi` | `"vi"` | now honors an explicit override instead of overwriting it |

:::

::: {.notes}
Most defaults stayed put, because they were already the right choice for
that family.
:::

## 3. The analytic covariance: an exact standard error {.sectionbreak}

![](images/sec-analytic.jpg){.nostretch}

::: {.notes}
The last piece is `covMethod="analytic"` itself, and this one is Hidde's.
Hidde van de Beek led the work that makes it possible.
:::

## The exact gradient stops one derivative short of a standard error

```{=html}
<svg class="dg" viewBox="0 0 1000 320" role="img"
     aria-label="The population objective is a data term plus a log-determinant penalty term. The gradient, already exact, needs second-order sensitivities. The observed information -- one more derivative -- needs third-order sensitivities, and only in the log-determinant term.">
  <rect x="40" y="60" width="430" height="200" rx="8" fill="#eef2f6" stroke="#8fa0b6" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text class="lab" x="255" y="94" text-anchor="middle">gradient (already exact)</text>
  <text class="t" x="255" y="140" text-anchor="middle">data term + log-determinant term</text>
  <text class="sm" x="255" y="170" text-anchor="middle">one derivative in</text>
  <rect x="90" y="192" width="330" height="40" rx="6" fill="#e6f0da" stroke="#4a7d18" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text class="mono grn" x="255" y="217" text-anchor="middle">needs 2nd-order sensitivities</text>

  <line x1="500" y1="160" x2="560" y2="160" stroke="#6b7b90" stroke-width="2.5" marker-end="url(#ar4)"/>
  <defs>
    <marker id="ar4" markerWidth="10" markerHeight="10" refX="7" refY="5" orient="auto">
      <path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#6b7b90"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>
  <text class="sm" x="530" y="145" text-anchor="middle">one more</text>
  <text class="sm" x="530" y="180" text-anchor="middle">derivative</text>

  <rect x="570" y="60" width="410" height="210" rx="8" fill="#eef2f6" stroke="#8fa0b6" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text class="lab" x="775" y="94" text-anchor="middle">observed information (new, "analytic")</text>
  <text class="t" x="775" y="136" text-anchor="middle">same two terms, differentiated again</text>
  <rect x="600" y="148" width="350" height="32" rx="6" fill="#e6f0da" stroke="#4a7d18" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text class="sm grn" x="775" y="169" text-anchor="middle">data term: needs nothing new</text>
  <rect x="600" y="188" width="350" height="60" rx="6" fill="#f3dede" stroke="#b40000" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text class="mono red" x="775" y="208" text-anchor="middle">log-det term:</text>
  <text class="mono red" x="775" y="230" text-anchor="middle">needs 3rd-order sensitivities</text>
</svg>
```

::: {.notes}
For the new analytic method the population objective is a data term
plus a log determinant penalty term. The gradient -- already exact,
from the Almquist sensitivity equations only needs second order
sensitivities. The observed information is one more derivative past
that. The data term needs nothing new. But the log determinant term
needs third order sensitivities, and that's confined to exactly that
one term.
:::

## A finite-differenced Hessian has a harder accuracy floor than a gradient

- A finite-differenced **gradient**'s achievable accuracy scales with the
  inner-problem tolerance to the two-thirds power
- A finite-differenced **Hessian**'s achievable accuracy is worse -- it
  only scales to the one-half power
- ... and it needs a step size tuned by hand: too large and you get
  truncation bias, too small and round-off makes it erratic -- sometimes
  not even positive definite

::: rule
:::

The analytic form carries **no step size** -- it is limited only by the
accuracy of the sensitivity and ODE solutions underneath it.

::: {.notes}
The analytic gradient has no step size and no finite difference noise,
so it is not erratic or biased -- it is exact.  It is only limited by
the accuracy of the ODE systems themselves.
:::

## On warfarin data, the analytic value matches NONMEM -- with no step to tune

```{=html}
<svg class="dg" viewBox="0 0 1000 340" role="img"
     aria-label="Standard error against finite-difference step size for one warfarin model parameter. The analytic value is a flat horizontal line. The finite-difference value only tracks it over a narrow middle band of step sizes, and is biased or erratic at the extremes.">
  <line x1="80" y1="280" x2="940" y2="280" stroke="#0f243e" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <polygon points="940,280 928,274 928,286" fill="#0f243e"/>

        fill="none" stroke="#b40000" stroke-width="2.5"/>

```

::: {.smaller}
Warfarin PK, one-compartment oral absorption, 10 subjects, correlated
clearance/volume random-effect block, diagonal absorption-rate random
effect -- the analytic standard error matches an independent NONMEM run
to every figure shown.
:::

::: {.notes}
On a warfarin case study -- one compartment, oral absorption, ten
subjects, a correlated random effect block on clearance and volume, and a
diagonal random effect on the absorption rate -- the analytic standard
error matched an independent NONMEM run to every figure they reported.
The finite difference standard error only tracked that value over a
narrow middle band of step sizes -- too large a step and it's biased, too
small and it gets erratic. The analytic value just sits there, flat, no
step size involved at all.
:::

## Why this matters

:::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
- The default covariance step now covers every estimated theta,
  residual-error parameters included
- `sa`, `imp`, `analytic` and the finite-difference methods now travel
  across mixed-effects fits, switchable after the fact with `setCov()`
- `covMethod="analytic"` gives you an exact standard error with no
  finite-difference step size to tune
:::

::: {.column width="48%" .checks}
- Spot-check an `"r,s"` covariance against `"analytic"` or `"sa"`
  without paying for a second fit
- The covariance step you gave up on for `npag`/`npb` is worth trying
  again -- it's there now
- Tell us where the analytic covariance falls outside its scope
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
To summarize: the default covariance step now covers:

- every estimated parameter, SA, IMP, analytic and the finite-difference methods.

- you can switch after the fact with set cov

- the analytic covariance gives you an exact standard error.

:::
